title: How we translate wastewater into estimates of drug consumption

# How we translate wastewater into estimates of drug consumption


### A walk through the math


[Kait Hess Jimenez, MS](https://substack.com/@kaithessjimenez)


and[Josh Harrison](https://substack.com/@harrisonjg)


Nov 02, 2026


*By Kaitlyn Hess Jimenez, MS, Josh Harrison, PhD, and Maxim Imakaev, PhD*


As we shared previously, this fall Biobot is launching a new tool for public health practitioners to translate wastewater data into figures that inform substance use within their communities: the Biobot Substance Use Calculator. To build this tool, we dug through over 350 papers to understand substance use behavior and drug metabolism.


Our calculator gives you access to this research. We provide recommended parameters for linking wastewater to substance use, and all these parameters can be modified to reflect the idiosyncrasies of your community. To make best use of the calculator, it is important to understand the rationale and mathematics that we harnessed. In this post, we will go step-by-step through our calculations.


## What does the calculator do?


**At its core, the calculator converts the amount of a marker (like a drug or metabolite) in wastewater to the amount of a substance that was consumed** .


Fig. 1 The process for estimating drug users, doses per day, and other consumption metrics. We start with an inflow sample and obtain LCMS-based measurements of markers related to consumption of a substance. After quality control related analysis and normalization, the data are input into the consumption calculations.


The markers reflect what the body excretes after a substance is consumed, usually a metabolite, and for some substances, such as methamphetamine, the drug itself. For instance, when a person ingests fentanyl (the parent compound) the body processes that drug, and excretes norfentanyl (the metabolite). Thus, norfentanyl is a marker that conveys information about how much fentanyl was consumed.


The math we use for the conversion is quite simple (Eq. 1):


The marker load is the marker concentration times a per-person volume of water, associated with your community’s wastewater sample. The molar-mass ratio, which is static for each parent/marker pair, turns grams of a marker into grams of a parent drug. The excretion fraction, based on human metabolism cited in literature, is the share of the absorbed dose that the body expels as that marker.


To state this in another way, we need to understand the total amount of mass excreted by a person (the load), account for the relationship between parent and metabolite compounds, and account for losses during metabolism.


This absorbed mass can then be further transformed in a few useful ways. We can convert the mass to:


-


Doses per day


-


Number of users


-


The amount of a substance purchased and its street dollar value


The calculations for each of these conversions are as follows (Eqs. 2–4):


We will go through each of these calculations in more detail below.


## The challenge that the calculator solves


The literature describes many of the values that we substitute into Eqs. 1–4, but rarely provides consensus. Indeed, we have observed that publications often differ in the methodology they use to estimate the same parameter. For instance, we found eight different ways excretion factors were measured: from radiolabeled mass balance in urine and feces to the share of an administered dose recovered in urine over varying time periods (from 12 hours to three days). Sometimes excretion factors account for bioavailability, sometimes not.


We read through all of these various methods and chose the parameters that avoid inaccuracies in our mathematics above. Within the calculator interface, we provide a range of values that reflect the real world variation we observed in the literature. Moreover, the calculator automatically performs calculations from this range of reasonable values to provide an estimate of variation around a particular calculation.


We also ensure that all of the parameters in the calculator are compatible with each other. For example, the calculator provides the estimated mass of drug base (free base). Drug purity in the US is frequently measured as salt, not free base. Applying salt-basis purity to the mass of drug base would be incorrect. To resolve this, we convert salt-basis purity to the drug-base-basis, and provide instructions on how to do this conversion for your own catchment.


## Term by term: how to understand each component of our equations


### Excretion factor


Let’s start with the excretion factor. This is the share of an absorbed dose that the body expels as the marker. Because it is measured against the absorbed dose rather than the amount taken, it is a ‘systemic’ excretion factor. We use a molar basis for this factor, meaning we are comparing the parent to metabolite in terms of actual molecules. Note that we have a separate term in Eq. 1 for the mass ratio between parents and metabolites (molar mass of parent ÷ molar mass of marker). The excretion factors used reflect total excretion. Some studies only measured excretion over a few hours, which is not enough time to excrete an entire dose for many substances.


### Bioavailability


In our calculator, bioavailability is a fraction of the consumed drug that reached the bloodstream. Bioavailability accounts for losses during consumption. For example, if a substance is smoked, a portion of it is lost from failure to inhale all the smoke, pipe or foil residue, and breakdown from heat. Injected use is by definition 100% bioavailability.


We extensively searched the literature to estimate bioavailability for each route of ingestion (smoking, snorting, injecting), and computed bioavailability that is representative of a typical mix. For many drugs, the use pattern also changes geographically. For example, smoking meth is more common in the West, while injecting is more common in the East. In the “About the target” section we provide recommended values for different regions—for methamphetamine, it would be 50% in the West to 60% in the East, because injection use is more common in the East. Public health practitioners familiar with their communities’ behavior can modify bioavailability to make estimates more accurate, and the “Methodology” section describes how to do it. It is not a simple average but a weighted geometric average, because the least efficient route contributes more.


### Dosage


Every dose we describe is converted to an absorbed dose (what reached the bloodstream) of pure drug at 100% purity. What is consumed is always more than the absorbed dose; how much more varies by drug, route of administration, and dilution by cutting agents. For example, for fentanyl smoked from foil, 100mg of street powder at 5% street purity, delivers only 3mg to the blood—33 times less than the nominal street dose.


### Street purity


The way we define street purity includes the salt-to-base factor. For instance, the purity of methamphetamine is capped at 80.4% because the street product is hydrochloride, a salt. There are a few caveats about purity. Dealer (wholesale) purity is typically higher than the street purity because the drug is cut further before the retail sale. Purity from drug seizures is often a mix of the two depending on when and where the drug was seized. Second, in the United States, purity is often reported as salt, without the salt-to-base factor, so it must be adjusted before its application in our calculator. We describe how to do this in the “Methodology” section of the calculator.


## Steps of the calculator in detail


### Calculating number of doses


Once we have calculated the absorbed mass (Eq. 1) we can estimate doses per day with Eq. 2:


The divisor in Eq. 2 can be varied in our calculator to reflect different types of doses. For instance, a medical dose, a lethal dose for a naive user, or a ‘heavy’ dose from a habituated user. Dose estimates are challenging to come by as survey data are few and may be based on inaccurate reports of dose or substance. The dose tiers that we have collected are from a variety of sources, including traffic stops, surveys, and toxicology reports from overdoses.


### Calculating number of use-days


A use-day is a day on which an individual consumed a particular substance. For example, if there are 100 heavy users who use a drug on 50% of the days, and 500 light users who use a drug on 10% of the days then every day this community will see 100 use-days: 100 x 0.5 + 500 x 0.1 = 100, with 100 heavy users contributing 50 use-days, and 500 light users contributing another 50. We usually work with use-days per day.


To estimate number of use-days, from wastewater we use Eq. 3:


The key component of this is the ‘average amount’ used per use day. The absorbed mass calculated from Eq. 1 is the total over all users that contributed to wastewater. Thus, we must divide that by the average amount used per day across users. If we were to divide by the average amount used for some specific user group, say light users, then it would only capture a portion of the total mass that was recovered from the sewer and our calculations would be incorrect. We would estimate many more users than there are because heavy users may contribute disproportionately to the waste stream.


### Calculating number of users


If we know the number of use-days, estimating the number of users is simple:


It is easy to understand why this step is necessary. Equation 3 says: we find 100 daily doses of a drug in the community every day. But the users don’t use the drug every day. If an average user only uses the drug one day in five, then 100 daily doses a day means 500 users in total.


An average here would be plain population mean over the whole user group. Coming back to our example: 100 users use the drug on 50% of the days, and 500 use on 10%—the average use frequency is (100 x 50% + 500 x 10%) / (100 + 500) = 16.6% - the average user uses the drug on 16.6% of the days, one day in 6. Note that it is closer to a light user frequency, 10% , because there are more light users. Separating heavy and light users requires a different calculation.


Applying these numbers, we get: 100 use-days per day ÷ 16.6% use frequency = 600 users. Because an average user uses on one day in 6, then 100 daily use-days means 600 users. Exactly what we started with (100 heavy and 500 light users).


### Estimating users for a specific group


For cocaine and methamphetamine, the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) reports how often do people use the drug. The surveys typically partition users into groups such as “past-month user” - anyone who used a drug in the past month. The two most common groups are “past-year” and “past-month”, and sometimes a “daily or near daily” group is added. Note that “past-year user” means essentially any user, because it includes anyone who used the drug in the last year, even if only a few times. Past-month are a subset of past-year, not necessarily “heavy” users, but regular users.


In our example of an imaginary town, we have 100 “heavy” users who use the drug on 50% of the days, and we have 600 of “past-year” users, anyone who used the drug, heavy and light combined. This broadest group, “past-year users” used on 16.6% of the days.


What if we wanted to know the number of heavy users? We could change the fraction of days used in Eq. 4 from 16.6% to 50%, but that would give us 100 / 50% = 200 heavy users, which is double of what what we started with. The reason is that heavy users account for only 50% of the use-days. So we should modify our equation:


Applying it to our imaginary town, we get 100 x 0.5 / 0.5 = 100 heavy users, and 100 x 1 / 0.166 = 600 total users. The share of use-days for the largest group, past-year users, is 1 by definition.


It is crucial that both terms, the share of use-days and the frequency of use, come from the same source - most likely, the NSDUH survey or a similar study.


There is no NSDUH data for fentanyl. What’s more, the existing studies suggest there is no casual use of fentanyl. Past-year use frequency for fentanyl is 72%—users who used fentanyl in the past year have used it 5 times a week. For cocaine this number is 16%—once a week, which is believable. A high past-year use frequency suggests that the use tiers have collapsed: any user of fentanyl is a frequent user. This is likely due to the extremely addictive nature of fentanyl. Another reason is that those who consume fentanyl often began by taking heroin or prescription opioids, so they are opioid-dependent and using near-daily when they start. We define no use tiers for fentanyl for this reason.


Of course, survey data is not unbiased. NSDUH is a household survey, so it reaches people who are unhoused or incarcerated poorly, and these are often the most frequent users. True frequency of use is therefore likely higher than the survey suggests, which means user counts built on survey frequencies are more likely too high than too low. These caveats aside, the national survey is our best source for understanding how often people use drugs.


## Calculating the street value of substances consumed


This calculation (Eq. 6) is a bit more straightforward than estimating users (Eq. 3):


Bioavailability reflects route of ingestion (e.g., smoking is an inefficient way to consume the most mass of a substance) and purity reflects how much of the street product is actually the drug, including the base-to-salt ratio. Once we have a purchased mass, we can multiply it by a street price per gram. Our default prices come from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime for cocaine and from a San Francisco street study for fentanyl; for methamphetamine there is no good national figure, so the default is an estimate. Prices vary widely by place, so a local price should be used where one is available.


Information regarding how much Americans spend on illegal drugs is sparse. The last estimate was RAND’s


*What America’s Users Spend on Illegal Drugs* that covered 2006-2016.


## Putting this all together: recommendations for use


Estimating substance use is challenging but critical for our nation’s health! We are certain that wastewater plays a critical role in understanding usage patterns—most people contribute to the waste-stream, so it is unbiased, it protects individual privacy, and it is inexpensive.


Our calculator provides the necessary link from wastewater to real-world metrics: numbers of users, total amount of a substance purchased, and the number of doses consumed. We hope and anticipate that users of the calculator will follow our curated path through the calculations to better understand what is happening in their communities.


We plan to launch the calculator in a matter of weeks—please stay tuned!
